lede: A Missouri printer's boy and Mississippi steamboat pilot who took a riverman's call for a pen name, made the world laugh, went broke, paid back every cent by lecturing around the globe, and wrote the novel that Hemingway said all modern American literature comes from.

ps: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in Florida, Missouri, on 30 November 1835, and grew up in the river town of Hannibal. As Mark Twain he became the most famous American writer of his time.

He worked as a printer, a steamboat pilot, a silver miner and a newspaper reporter before a comic story about a jumping frog made his name in 1865. His books include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884 to 1885).
He was also a star lecturer, a failed investor, and in later life a fierce critic of racism, imperialism and greed. He died at his home in Redding, Connecticut, on 21 April 1910.
His family moved to Hannibal, on the Mississippi, when he was nearly four. The town, the river, the caves and the islands became St. Petersburg in Tom Sawyer.

Missouri was a slave state. His family owned an enslaved woman for a time, and his uncle's farm, where he spent boyhood summers, had enslaved workers. He later said that as a boy he had seen nothing wrong with slavery.
His father, a judge and struggling storekeeper, died in 1847. Sam left school and was apprenticed to a printer. In his late teens he worked as a printer in St. Louis, New York and Philadelphia.

In 1857 he began training as a Mississippi steamboat pilot under Horace Bixby, learning every bend and snag of more than a thousand miles of river. He was licensed in 1859. His younger brother Henry died after a steamboat explosion in 1858, a loss he blamed himself for.

1861: the Civil War closed the river. He served about two weeks in a Confederate volunteer unit that broke up, then went west to Nevada with his brother Orion, who had been made secretary of the territory.

1862 to 1864: after failing as a silver miner he became a reporter for the Territorial Enterprise in Virginia City. In February 1863 he first signed himself Mark Twain, the riverman's call for two fathoms, safe water.
November 1865: his story of Jim Smiley and his jumping frog appeared in a New York paper and was reprinted across the country.
1867 to 1869: he sailed to Europe and the Holy Land on the steamship Quaker City and mocked American tourists and old-world pieties in The Innocents Abroad (1869), a bestseller.

1870: he married Olivia Langdon, called Livy, the daughter of a wealthy, anti-slavery family in Elmira, New York. In 1874 they moved into a large, ornate house in Hartford, Connecticut, where he wrote his best-known books.
1876 and 1884 to 1885: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, then Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, published in Britain in December 1884 and in the United States in February 1885.
1885 to 1886: his own publishing firm brought out the memoirs of the former president Ulysses S. Grant, who finished them days before dying of cancer. They earned Grant's widow a fortune.

1894 to 1898: failed investments, above all a typesetting machine, and the collapse of his publishing firm left him bankrupt. He set out on a lecture tour around the world, through Australia, India and South Africa, and by 1898 had paid his creditors in full.
1896 to 1909: his daughter Susy died of meningitis in 1896, Livy in 1904, and his daughter Jean on Christmas Eve 1909. He died of heart failure four months later.
The Innocents Abroad (1869), Roughing It (1872) on his years in the West, and Life on the Mississippi (1883) on his piloting days.
The Gilded Age (1873), written with Charles Dudley Warner, a satire of greed and corruption whose title became the name of the era.

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), a boyhood comedy, and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884 to 1885), told in Huck's own voice as he and Jim, a man escaping slavery, travel down the Mississippi on a raft.

A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889), about a factory foreman knocked back in time, and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), a dark story of babies swapped across the colour line, solved by fingerprints.
Later essays and stories attacked imperialism and religion, and his long, rambling Autobiography was published in full only from 2010.
Olivia Langdon Clemens (1845 to 1904), his wife, first reader and editor. Their children were Langdon, who died as a baby, Susy, Clara and Jean.
William Dean Howells (1837 to 1920), novelist and editor, his closest literary friend.
Ulysses S. Grant (1822 to 1885), the Civil War general and president whose memoirs he published.
Henry H. Rogers (1840 to 1909), the Standard Oil executive who sorted out his finances after the bankruptcy.
Helen Keller (1880 to 1968), whom he met when she was fourteen. He admired her deeply and helped raise money for her education.
Nikola Tesla (1856 to 1943), a friend whose New York laboratory he visited in the 1890s.
He lived from the age of steamboats and slavery to the age of telephones and cars. After the Civil War came Reconstruction, then the return of white rule and segregation laws across the South.
The Gilded Age was a time of railways, vast fortunes, crooked politics and huge immigration. Newspapers and lecture halls made writers into public celebrities, and he was among the first.
From 1901 he was a vice-president of the Anti-Imperialist League and condemned the American war in the Philippines and Belgian King Leopold's rule in the Congo.

He showed that American speech, with all its slang and dialects, could carry great literature. Ernest Hemingway wrote that 'all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn'.

Huckleberry Finn uses a racist slur for Black people more than 200 times, as people in that time and place spoke. Many readers see the book as an attack on racism, through Huck's choice to help Jim; others find it painful and harmful in classrooms. Both views are argued today.
His Hartford house and his boyhood home in Hannibal are museums, and the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor has been awarded since 1998.

myths.c: He came in and went out with Halley's Comet.
myths.t: The comet was near the Sun when he was born in 1835 and returned in April 1910, when he died. He had predicted it in 1909, saying he expected to go out with it, according to his biographer Albert Bigelow Paine.

myths.c: He said 'Reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.'
myths.t: In 1897 an American reporter in London checked a rumour that he was dying. His note said 'the report of my death was an exaggeration'. The punchier version grew later.

myths.c: Huckleberry Finn was banned only in recent times.
myths.t: In 1885 the public library of Concord, Massachusetts, removed it as rough and vulgar. Since the 1950s it has been challenged mainly for its racial language.

myths.c: Mark Twain is a riverboat term.
myths.t: Leadsmen called 'mark twain' when the line showed two fathoms, twelve feet, safe depth for a steamboat.
